title: How to Leave the Ground
subtitle: Wings, balloons, jets, rockets and the road to Mars
subject: Physics

p: Wave your hand through the air. It feels like nothing is there. But air has weight. One cubic metre of it, a box about the size of a washing machine, has a mass of 1.2 kilograms. The air in an ordinary classroom weighs more than 200 kilograms, about three grown adults. The whole atmosphere presses down on every square metre of ground with a force of 10 tonnes.

This is the secret of flight. You cannot fly in nothing. Every bird, bee, balloon and aeroplane stays up by pushing on air, and air, because it has mass, pushes back. The only flying machines that do not need air are rockets, and they carry their own stuff to push against.
Stick your hand out of a car window at 100 kilometres per hour and tilt it slightly. Feel it lift. That is a wing, and you just discovered the whole idea. The rest of this book is details.
pages.cap: Air moving over a tilted hand, or a wing, gets pushed down. The hand gets pushed up.
pages.fact: Did you know? A hummingbird's heart beats up to 1,200 times a minute while it hovers, and it burns energy so fast it is always a few hours from starving.

p: Anything that flies is in a tug of war between four forces. Weight pulls it down, because gravity never stops. Lift pushes it up. Drag pulls it backwards as the air resists being shoved aside. Thrust pushes it forward.

To take off, lift must beat weight. To speed up, thrust must beat drag. To cruise at a steady height and speed, all four are balanced: lift equals weight, thrust equals drag. An airliner at 900 kilometres per hour is not fighting hard; it is in balance, like a swimmer holding position in a river.

Each flying thing picks a different way to win. A bird gets both lift and thrust from flapping. A plane gets lift from fixed wings and thrust from engines. A balloon does not bother with lift from motion at all: it is simply lighter than the air it sits in. A rocket ignores the air and uses raw thrust against its own weight. Four forces, many answers.
pages.cap: Lift against weight, thrust against drag. Steady flight means both pairs balance.

pages.h: To fly, push air down. The air pushes you up.
p: Wings, rotor blades, flapping feathers and buzzing insect wings all do the same job: throwing air at the ground.

A wing is a shape that makes air go down. Tilt a flat board into the wind and air hits the bottom and bounces downward; the board is pushed up. A real wing does that and more. Its curved top makes the air flowing over it bend down and speed up as it follows the curve. Faster air has lower pressure, so the pressure on top of the wing drops. Higher pressure below, lower pressure above: the wing is lifted.

Both descriptions are true at once. Newton's third law says the wing pushes air down, so the air pushes the wing up. Bernoulli's principle says faster air has lower pressure. They are two ways of looking at the same event.

One popular explanation is wrong: that air over the top must 'catch up' with air underneath. It does not. Wind tunnel tests show the top air arrives far earlier. Tilt the wing too steeply, about 15 degrees, and the air stops following the curve and tumbles. Lift collapses. Pilots call that a stall.
pages.cap: Air bends down over the curved top; pressure drops there; the wing rises.

p: Push through air and it pushes back. That is drag, and it has a cruel rule: it grows with the square of your speed. Go twice as fast and the drag is four times bigger. Go three times as fast and it is nine times bigger. This is why a bike at 30 kilometres per hour is mostly fighting air, not the road, and why cars burn so much more fuel on the highway.

Shape matters enormously. A flat plate facing the wind has about ten times the drag of a smooth teardrop of the same width. That is why planes, fast trains, dolphins and falcons are all pointed at the front and taper at the back.

Drag is also what saves a skydiver. Falling, you speed up until drag equals your weight; then you stop accelerating. Spread out flat, a person reaches that balance at about 200 kilometres per hour. Open a parachute, drag soars, and the balance speed drops to about 20. Same force, bigger surface.
pages.cap: A parachute has about 100 times the drag area of a falling body, so the balance speed drops ten times.

pages.q: A plane doubles its speed. What happens to the drag from the air?
pages.why: Drag grows with the square of speed: two times the speed means two times two, or four times the drag.

pages.h: Thrust: propellers are wings that spin
p: Lift explains how a wing holds a plane up, but something has to keep the air flowing over the wing in the first place. That is thrust. The oldest way to make it is the propeller.

Look closely at a propeller blade and you will see a wing: curved on one side, flatter on the other, and twisted along its length. When it spins, each blade is a wing moving sideways through the air. It makes 'lift', but pointing forward. In other words, a propeller throws air backwards, and the plane is pushed forward. Boat propellers do the same in water. A hand-held fan is a propeller that stays still and moves the air instead.

Propellers are efficient at low speeds, which is why small planes, drones and most airships still use them. But a blade tip moving faster than sound loses its grip on the air, so above about 700 kilometres per hour, propellers run out of pull. For that, you need a jet.
pages.cap: An engine's spin reaches the propeller through shafts and gears; the blades throw air backwards.

pages.h: Twelve seconds that changed the world
p: On 17 December 1903, on a cold beach at Kitty Hawk in North Carolina, Orville Wright lay flat on the lower wing of a machine of spruce and cotton, opened the engine, and flew for 12 seconds. He covered 37 metres, shorter than the wingspan of a modern airliner. By the end of the day, his brother Wilbur had stayed up for 59 seconds and 260 metres.

Others had built gliders and engines. What the Wrights solved was control. They noticed that birds twist their wingtips to turn, and built wires that let the pilot twist the wings the same way. They also tested more than 200 wing shapes in a home-built wind tunnel, because the published tables of lift turned out to be wrong.
Sixty-six years later, in 1969, people walked on the Moon. Orville Wright, who died in 1948, lived to see jet aircraft. Few inventions have gone from zero to everywhere so fast.
pages.cap: From a 12-second hop to the Moon in one lifetime.

pages.h: Try it: test a wing on a paper plane
p: Change one thing at a time and watch what the air does.
steps: Fold a simple dart paper plane. Throw it gently, straight ahead, five times, and note how far it goes.
Fold the back edge of each wing up by about 5 millimetres. Throw it again. The nose should rise and it may loop or stall. Those bent edges work like the elevators on a real tail.
Bend the edges down instead. Now it should dive. Set them flat again.
Bend only the left wing's edge up. The plane rolls and turns. That is what the Wright brothers' wing-twisting did.
Add a paper clip to the nose. It flies straighter and faster: more weight up front keeps the wing at a steady angle to the air.
pages.cap: Tiny bends at the back edge of a wing steer the whole plane.
pages.safe: Throw away from faces; paper plane noses are sharper than they look.

p: Birds have been flying for about 150 million years, and they are the dinosaurs that survived. Everything about them is built for it. Their bones are hollow, with struts inside like a bridge. A frigatebird with a 2-metre wingspan has a skeleton that weighs less than its feathers. Their lungs push air through in one direction, so they get oxygen on both the in-breath and the out-breath, which is why bar-headed geese can fly over the Himalayas at 7,000 metres where people can barely walk.

A wing beat is two moves. On the downstroke the wing pushes air down and back, making both lift and thrust. On the upstroke the feathers part slightly to let air through, like opening blinds, so the bird is not pushed back down.

The champions are specialists. An albatross locks its 3.5-metre wings and glides for days on ocean wind, barely flapping. A peregrine falcon folds its wings and dives at 390 kilometres per hour, the fastest animal on Earth. An Arctic tern flies about 70,000 kilometres a year, pole to pole and back.
pages.cap: Feathered dinosaurs were already flying when the asteroid struck 66 million years ago. Their descendants are birds.

pages.h: Bees, flies and the vortex trick
p: For a long time, engineers joked that bees should not be able to fly: their wings seemed too small for their fat bodies. The joke was wrong, and finding out why took high-speed cameras.

A honeybee beats its wings about 230 times a second, which is what makes the buzz. Each wing does not just flap up and down. It flips over at the end of every stroke and sweeps back, like a swimmer's hand. As the wing slices forward, a tiny tornado of air rolls up along its front edge and sits on top of the wing. That spinning air has very low pressure, and it sucks the wing upward. Engineers call it a leading-edge vortex. Big planes avoid it. Insects live on it.

Dragonflies take it further. They move their four wings independently and can hover, fly backwards and hit 50 kilometres per hour. The smallest flying insects, fairyflies, are 0.2 millimetres long and row through the air as if it were syrup, with wings that are just bristles.
pages.cap: Each wing stroke rolls up a tiny spinning vortex that lifts the bee.

p: The first people to leave the ground did not use wings at all. On 21 November 1783, two Frenchmen rose over Paris in a paper-and-cloth balloon built by the Montgolfier brothers, with a fire of straw underneath. They flew for 25 minutes.

A balloon flies because of a simple rule: a thing floats if it weighs less than the air it pushes aside. Hot air at 100 degrees Celsius is about one-quarter lighter than cold air, so a cubic metre of it can lift about 300 grams. That is why hot-air balloons are huge: a balloon carrying three people holds about 3,000 cubic metres of hot air.

Helium is better. It is about seven times lighter than air, so one cubic metre lifts about 1 kilogram. Hydrogen lifts slightly more but burns, which is why giant hydrogen airships stopped flying after the Hindenburg caught fire in 1937. Today, helium balloons carry telescopes to 35 kilometres, above 99 percent of the air, where the sky is black at noon.
pages.cap: Floating in air works like floating in water: be lighter than what you push aside.

pages.q: Why does a hot-air balloon rise?
opts: Hot air pushes against the ground
The air inside is lighter than the cooler air outside
Heat makes the balloon fabric lighter
pages.why: Heating air makes it expand and thin out; the balloon then weighs less than the cold air it displaces, so it floats up.

pages.h: Gliders and the free ride in the sky
p: An aeroplane with no engine is a glider, and a good one is astonishing. Modern sailplanes have long thin wings and can travel 60 metres forward for every 1 metre they drop. Released at 1,000 metres, one could glide 60 kilometres in still air.

But the air is not still. The Sun heats fields and car parks more than forests and lakes, and warm air rises from them in invisible columns called thermals, often at 2 to 5 metres per second. A glider pilot circles inside a thermal and goes up with it, the same way hawks and vultures do. On a good day, pilots climb to the base of the clouds, then glide to the next thermal. Flights of 1,000 kilometres with no engine happen every summer.

Wind blowing over a mountain ridge is pushed upward too, and so are waves of air far downwind. The glider altitude record, set in 2018 over Argentina, is 23,200 metres: higher than most spy planes, with no engine at all.
pages.cap: The Sun warms the ground, warm air rises in columns, and gliders and hawks ride them up.

pages.h: Jet engines: suck, squeeze, burn, blow
p: A jet engine is a tube that swallows air at the front and shoots it out the back faster than it came in. Pushing air backwards hard pushes the plane forwards. Inside, it happens in four steps that engineers summarize as suck, squeeze, burn, blow.

A huge fan at the front sucks air in. Rows of spinning blades, the compressor, squeeze it to about 40 times normal pressure. Fuel is sprayed in and burns continuously, heating the gas to around 1,500 degrees Celsius, hotter than the melting point of the metal blades, which survive only because they are hollow and cooled from inside. The hot gas then blasts through a turbine, which spins the compressor and the fan, and out the back.

Here is the surprise: on a modern airliner, most of the push comes from the big front fan, not the hot exhaust. About 90 percent of the air goes around the hot core, not through it. That is why today's engines are so wide and so much quieter than the screaming jets of the 1960s.
pages.cap: Like a candle, a jet burns fuel with oxygen from the air; unlike a candle, it does it in a hurricane.

pages.h: A jumbo jet leaves the ground
p: A fully loaded Airbus A380 weighs up to 575 tonnes, about the same as 100 elephants or 400 cars. To get it into the air, four engines push it down a 3-kilometre runway until it reaches about 280 kilometres per hour. At that speed, its wings, which together cover 845 square metres, make enough lift to beat all that weight. The nose comes up, and 575 tonnes of metal, fuel and people leave the ground.

Then it climbs to about 11,000 metres. Up there the air is thin, which cuts drag and saves fuel, and the plane cruises at around 900 kilometres per hour. The outside temperature is about minus 55 degrees Celsius and there is so little oxygen that you would pass out in under a minute. The cabin is sealed and pumped up with air from the engines, so inside it feels like a mountain 2,000 metres high.
Across the Atlantic, the plane burns about 100 tonnes of fuel. It takes off heavy and lands light.
pages.cap: One loaded jumbo weighs about as much as 100 elephants.

pages.h: A loaded airliner weighs as much as 100 elephants. Air holds it up.
p: At 280 kilometres per hour, the wings throw enough air downward every second to lift all of it.

Sound travels through air at about 343 metres per second, roughly 1,235 kilometres per hour at sea level. A plane moving slower than that pushes a wave of pressure ahead of itself, warning the air it is coming. A plane moving faster arrives before its own sound. The air cannot get out of the way, so it piles up into a shock wave, a cone of squeezed air trailing behind the plane like the wake of a boat. When that cone sweeps over you, you hear a sonic boom.

The first person to do this on purpose was Chuck Yeager in 1947, in a rocket plane dropped from a bomber. The Concorde carried passengers from London to New York in three and a half hours at 2,180 kilometres per hour, from 1976 until 2003, but its booms were so loud it could only go fast over the ocean.

NASA's X-59 experimental jet, which first flew in late 2025, is shaped to spread its shock wave into a soft thump instead of a boom. Whether airlines will ever go supersonic again depends on the answer.
pages.cap: Pressure waves pile up into a cone when a plane outruns its own sound.

p: A helicopter has wings. They are just spinning. Each rotor blade is a long thin wing, and whirling it around at about 300 turns a minute keeps air flowing over it even when the helicopter is standing still. Tilt the whole spinning disc forward and some of the lift points forward too: that is how it moves. Tilt it back and it stops.
There is a catch. Spinning the rotor one way makes the body want to spin the other way. The little tail rotor pushes sideways to stop that. Lose the tail rotor and the helicopter spins.

The strangest helicopter ever built flew on Mars. Ingenuity, a 1.8-kilogram machine that arrived with NASA's Perseverance rover in 2021, had to fly in air only 1 percent as thick as Earth's. Its two rotors spun at 2,400 turns a minute, eight times faster than a normal helicopter's. It was meant to make five flights. It made 72 before it broke a blade in January 2024.
pages.cap: Ingenuity flew 72 times through Martian air thinner than at three times the height of Everest.

p: Everything so far has leaned on air. Rockets cannot, because where they are going there is none. Instead, a rocket carries its own stuff to throw. Burn fuel with oxygen, shoot the hot gas out the back at 3 to 4 kilometres per second, and the rocket is shoved the other way. Newton's third law: for every push, an equal push back. A rocket would work just as well in a vacuum as in air. In fact, it works better, because there is no drag.

The oxygen is the problem. A jet takes oxygen from the air, but a rocket must carry it, and oxygen is heavy. That is why a rocket on the launch pad is about 90 percent propellant by mass. The crew capsule on top is a tiny tip on a huge tank.
Stand near a launch and the numbers become feelings. A Falcon 9 produces 7.6 million newtons of thrust at lift-off; the sound alone could damage your hearing at 500 metres.
pages.cap: Hot gas out the back, rocket pushed forward: no air required.

pages.q: Which of these could still work in empty space with no air at all?
pages.why: A rocket pushes against its own exhaust, not the air. Propellers, rotors and balloons all need air to push on or float in.

pages.h: Orbit is about speed, not height
p: People imagine that spacecraft stay up because they are high, above gravity. Not so. At the height of the International Space Station, 400 kilometres up, gravity is still 89 percent as strong as on the ground. Throw a ball up there and it falls.

Isaac Newton explained orbit in 1687 with a thought experiment. Fire a cannon from a mountain top and the ball curves down to the ground. Fire it faster and it lands farther away. Fire it fast enough, and the ground curves away beneath it as quickly as it falls. The ball keeps falling but never lands. That is an orbit.

The speed needed near Earth is about 7.8 kilometres per second, 28,000 kilometres per hour, about 30 times the speed of a jet airliner. Getting that fast is nearly all of a rocket's job; getting high is the easy part. Once there, with no air to slow it, a satellite falls around the planet for years using no fuel at all.
pages.cap: Falling forever: the spacecraft drops toward Earth, but the ground keeps curving away.

p: For decades the biggest rocket ever to fly successfully was the Saturn V, which carried astronauts to the Moon from 1968 to 1972. It stood 111 metres tall, weighed 2,970 tonnes fuelled, and its five first-stage engines produced 35 million newtons of thrust. After two and a half minutes, the first stage fell into the ocean, used once and gone.

That throwing-away is why spaceflight has been so expensive. In 2015, SpaceX landed a Falcon 9 booster upright on its own fire, and began flying boosters again and again; some have now flown more than 25 times. The cost of putting a kilogram in orbit has fallen from tens of thousands of dollars to a few thousand.

Starship, 120 metres tall and about 5,000 tonnes fuelled, is designed to be fully reusable and to carry 100 tonnes to orbit. In test flights since 2023 it has both exploded and succeeded, including having its booster caught in mid-air by the launch tower's arms. It is not yet a finished machine.
pages.cap: A Saturn V on the pad: 35 million newtons about to push 2,970 tonnes off the ground.

pages.h: A house that falls around the world
p: The International Space Station is the largest thing people have ever built in space. It is as long as a football field, 109 metres, and has a mass of about 420 tonnes. It circles Earth at 400 kilometres up and 28,000 kilometres per hour, going right round in about 93 minutes. The crew see 16 sunrises every day.

People have lived aboard without a single break since 2 November 2000; more than 280 astronauts from over 20 countries have visited. Its solar panels make about 120 kilowatts of electricity, and water is recycled from sweat and urine until it is cleaner than most tap water.

Astronauts float, but not because there is no gravity. They float because the station and everyone inside are falling together, all the time. It is the same feeling as the top of a roller-coaster drop, held for six months. The station is planned to be guided into the Pacific Ocean around 2030, when its parts are worn out.
pages.cap: The station crosses the night side of Earth in 45 minutes, then back into sunlight.

p: Make thrust the way a rocket does: by throwing stuff out the back.
steps: Thread a 5-metre string through a drinking straw. Tie the string tight between two chairs.
Blow up a balloon and hold the neck pinched shut. Tape the balloon to the straw with the neck pointing at one chair.
Let go. The escaping air is thrown backwards; the balloon is pushed forwards along the string.
Try a long thin balloon against a round one, and a half-full balloon against a full one. Which goes farthest? More air thrown out faster means more thrust, exactly as in a real rocket.
pages.cap: The balloon does not push against the chairs or the air in front. It pushes against the air leaving it.
pages.safe: Keep balloons away from small children and pets; popped pieces are a choking hazard.

p: Six months of falling does strange things to a body. On Earth, your bones and muscles work against gravity every second. In orbit they do not, and the body stops bothering to maintain them. Astronauts lose about 1 percent of their bone mass every month, like fast ageing, and their leg muscles shrink. To fight it, they exercise about two hours a day strapped to treadmills and pulling on elastic cords.
Fluids float upward too. Faces puff up, legs get thin, and many astronauts' eyeballs flatten slightly, blurring their vision in ways doctors still do not fully understand.

Daily life needs rethinking. Water does not pour; it forms wobbling balls that stick to things, so drinks come in bags with straws. Sleep means zipping into a bag tied to a wall. Crumbs float into air filters, so bread is replaced by tortillas. Tears do not fall; they pool on your eye until you wipe them. The record for one stay is 437 days.
pages.cap: Without weight to carry, a skeleton in orbit quietly thins by about 1 percent a month.

p: To reach orbit you need 7.8 kilometres per second. To leave Earth entirely, never to fall back, you need 11.2 kilometres per second, about 40,000 kilometres per hour. That is escape velocity. Reach it, and Earth's gravity can slow you but never stop you.

The Moon is the nearest place to go: 384,000 kilometres away, about three days by rocket. Twelve people walked on it between 1969 and 1972, and nobody has since. NASA's Artemis program is changing that. In April 2026, four astronauts, including Canada's Jeremy Hansen, flew around the Moon on Artemis II. A landing near its south pole, where ice hides in craters that never see sunlight, is planned next. Dates keep slipping; it is now expected around the end of the 2020s at the earliest.

Why go back? Water ice can be split into breathable oxygen and rocket fuel. The Moon's weak gravity, one-sixth of Earth's, makes it a cheap place to launch from. And it is practice. The real target is farther.
pages.cap: The Moon, born from a giant impact 4.5 billion years ago, is three days away by rocket.

pages.q: Why do astronauts float inside the space station?
opts: There is no gravity 400 kilometres up
The station and the astronauts are falling together around Earth
The air inside is too thin to hold them down
pages.why: Gravity up there is nearly as strong as on the ground; everything is simply in free fall at the same rate, so nothing presses on anything.

p: Mars is never close. At its nearest, it is 55 million kilometres away, about 140 times farther than the Moon; at its farthest, 400 million. Earth and Mars line up well only once every 26 months, so missions go in a rush and then wait two years. The trip takes 6 to 9 months each way, and a crew would need to stay about 18 months before the planets lined up for the return. A round trip is nearly three years.

Landing is the nightmare. Mars has an atmosphere, but only 1 percent as thick as Earth's: enough to burn a spacecraft arriving at 20,000 kilometres per hour, but not enough for parachutes alone. NASA's Perseverance rover used a heat shield, then a 21-metre parachute, then rockets, then was lowered on cables from a hovering 'sky crane', all within seven minutes with no help from Earth, which was 11 light-minutes away.
Perseverance weighs 1 tonne. A crew mission would need to land 20 to 100 tonnes. Nobody has done that yet.
pages.cap: Mars, a cold desert with 1 percent of our air. Rovers have landed. People have not.

p: Once you can fly on Earth and Mars, other skies open up. Saturn's moon Titan has an atmosphere four times thicker than ours and gravity one-seventh of ours, so flying there is easy: a person with strapped-on wings could flap into the air. NASA's Dragonfly, a car-sized nuclear-powered drone with eight rotors, is due to launch in 2028 and start hopping across Titan's dunes and methane lakes in 2034.

Venus is the opposite. Its surface is 460 degrees Celsius and crushed under 90 times Earth's air pressure, but 55 kilometres up, the temperature and pressure are almost Earth-like. Two Soviet balloons drifted there for two days in 1985, and engineers have sketched cloud cities floating above the acid.

Jupiter and Saturn have no surface at all, just deeper and deeper gas. Any flight there is a one-way dive. In 1995 the Galileo probe parachuted into Jupiter and sent data for 58 minutes before the pressure crushed it.
pages.cap: Titan, under Saturn's rings, has thick air and weak gravity: the easiest place in the solar system to fly.

p: For all the jets and rockets, flight still has holes in it. The biggest is turbulence, the chaotic swirling of air. Engineers can predict it roughly, but the exact mathematics of how smooth flow breaks into tumbling chaos is an unsolved problem; there is a million-dollar prize for anyone who can crack the equations behind it. That is why a plane can still hit a bump that no forecast saw.

Nobody fully knows how birds navigate. Migrating birds seem to sense Earth's magnetic field, perhaps with a light-sensitive protein in their eyes, but how that works at the level of atoms is still argued over.

And nobody knows whether people can safely make the trip to Mars. Outside Earth's magnetic shield, space is full of radiation; a round trip might give a crew as much radiation as several thousand chest X-rays, and the effect on the body over years is uncertain. The machines are nearly ready. The questions about the people are not.
pages.cap: Bats find their way by sound. How birds read Earth's magnetic field is still a mystery.

pages.h: Every flight is a loan from the air, or a push against your own fire.
p: Feathers, fabric, metal, flame: a few centuries of trying, and one law of motion underneath it all.

items: the upward force a wing makes by pushing air downward
the backward force of air resisting something moving through it
the forward push from a propeller, jet or rocket
when a wing is tilted too steeply, the air stops following it and lift collapses
a column of warm rising air that gliders and hawks use to climb
a small spinning swirl of air, like a tiny tornado
faster than the speed of sound, about 1,235 kilometres per hour at sea level
falling around a planet so fast that you never hit the ground
the speed needed to leave a planet's gravity for good: 11.2 kilometres per second for Earth
falling with nothing pushing back, which is why astronauts float
the fuel and oxygen a rocket carries and throws out the back

qs: Would you accept a seat on the first crewed flight to Mars, a trip of nearly three years with unknown risks? What would make you say yes or no?
Birds, bees, balloons and rockets all fly in different ways. Which one do you think is the most clever solution, and why?
If drag grows with the square of speed, is it ever worth building faster passenger planes? What else would you need to think about?
